summary: This Reading Rockets article by Louisa Moats and Carol Tolman, excerpted from the LETRS Module 1 text, explains the types of developmental reading disability. It describes three overlapping but distinct deficits: phonological deficit, processing speed/orthographic processing deficit, and comprehension deficit. It also covers the single- and double-deficit distinction and co-occurring problems such as attention issues and ADHD.
one_line: Overview of the three overlapping types of developmental reading disability: phonological, processing speed/orthographic, and comprehension deficits.
key_facts: Researchers have identified three kinds of developmental reading disabilities that often overlap but can be separate and distinct: phonological deficit, processing speed/orthographic processing deficit, and comprehension deficit.
For research purposes, 'reading impaired' children may be all those who score below the 30th percentile in basic reading skill.
About 70-80 percent of poor readers have trouble with accurate and fluent word recognition that originates with weaknesses in phonological processing.
The term dyslexic is most often applied to the group of poor readers with phonological processing weaknesses.
About 10-15 percent of poor readers are accurate but too slow in word recognition and text reading, with specific weaknesses in speed of word recognition and automatic recall of word spellings.
The processing speed/orthographic subgroup generally has milder difficulties with reading than students with phonological processing deficits.

About 10-15 percent of poor readers decode words better than they can comprehend the meanings of passages, and their problems stem from disorders of social reasoning, abstract verbal reasoning, or language comprehension.
If a student has a prominent weakness in either phonological or rapid print (naming-speed) processing, they are said to have a single deficit in word recognition.
A combination of phonological and naming-speed deficits is called a double deficit (Wolf & Bowers, 1999).
Double-deficit children are more common than single-deficit children and are also the most challenging to remediate.
Related problems in children with reading disabilities often include faulty pencil grip and letter formation, attention problems, anxiety, task avoidance, weak impulse control, and distractibility.
About 30 percent of all children with dyslexia also have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
Dr. Louisa Moats developed the professional development program LETRS for teachers and reading specialists.
The article is excerpted from Language Essentials for Teachers of Reading and Spelling (LETRS): The Challenge of Learning to Read (Module 1), published by Sopris West in 2009.
